t: What to eat in Naples, in the order of the day
d: Sfogliatella, fried pizza, pizza a portafoglio, cuoppo, babà and STG pizza: what to eat in Naples and when, with indicative prices and where sources disagree.
x: In Naples you can eat at any hour, but not everything suits every hour. The sfogliatella belongs to the morning, fried pizza wants to come straight from the oil, oven-baked pizza is an evening order, and a babà closes any day well. This guide puts the tastings in order, says roughly what they cost, and where the sources disagree it says so. In short. Breakfast with coffee and a sfogliatella, a fried pizza mid-morning, a pizza a portafoglio with a frittatina or a crocchè at lunch, a cuoppo or a babà in the afternoon, a proper sit-down pizza in the evening. About €20-30 per person (indicative) covers the full round. Prices and closing days change from place to place: check before you go. A margherita pizza: tomato, mozzarella, basil and a raised crust Photo: Valerio Capello at English Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 3.0 , Wikimedia Commons Breakfast Coffee and a sfogliatella Riccia or frolla: try both if there are two of you. It generally costs a couple of euros. Mid-morning Fried pizza Filled with ricotta, pork cracklings and pepper: eat it straight out of the oil. Lunch Pizza a portafoglio and a frittatina A margherita folded in four and a pasta frittata: two tastings for a few euros. Afternoon Cuoppo or mixed fry The paper cone of fried things is eaten while walking: crocchè, zeppole, rice balls. Evening Sit-down pizza Marinara or margherita, the two classics: arrive early to avoid the queue. After dinner Babà, fiocco di neve or ministeriale A sweet to finish: it depends on which pastry shop you pass. What do people eat for breakfast in Naples? Sfogliatella and coffee # Start with a sfogliatella, and two words are needed right away. The riccia is the shell-shaped one, made of very thin layers and crisp; the frolla is round, smooth and softer. According to Lost in Food the filling is the same: a cream of ricotta, semolina, eggs and sugar, with candied fruit. Naples Insider confirms the two kinds and says people argue about them without ever settling it: the most useful thing is to taste both. A sfogliatella riccia, cut open to show the ricotta and candied-fruit filling Photo: Saggittarius A, CC BY-SA 4.0 , Wikimedia Commons As for history, the sources tell two versions that do not coincide. Lost in Food says the original recipe goes back to 1600 and was born in the convent of Santa Rosa on the Amalfi Coast, and also says a famous pastry shop on Via Toledo claims to have invented it first. Those are stories, not documents, and we report them as such. As for where to go

t: Visiting Matera's Sassi: how to see them and when to go
d: The Sassi of Matera on foot in one day: a route through Sasso Barisano and Caveoso, the Casa Grotta, how to get there and when to go, with official sources.
x: You do not visit Matera with a map in your hand; you visit it with your feet. The Sassi are a city carved and built on the edge of a canyon, and the best way to understand them is to walk, climb, descend and pause in the few places you can really go inside. This guide puts one day in order, explains when to go and says plainly where the sources disagree. In short. The Sassi of Matera are best seen on foot in a day: start in Sasso Barisano, climb to the Civita and the Cathedral, then descend into Sasso Caveoso and the Casa Grotta di Vico Solitario. Spring and autumn are named as the best seasons. For the Crypt of Original Sin, booking is compulsory. The Sassi of Matera with the Cathedral on the Civita and the ravine in the background Photo: Gigi.Parentini, CC BY-SA 4.0 , Wikimedia Commons What the Sassi are, in a few lines # According to the UNESCO entry, the property of the Sassi and the Park of the Rupestrian Churches comprises houses, churches, monasteries and hermitages built into the natural caves of the Murgia, covering 1,016 hectares, with more than a thousand dwellings and many workshops. Occupation goes back to the Palaeolithic and intensifies from the 8th century. There are two Sassi, Barisano and Caveoso, and between them lies the Civita, the first inhabited nucleus, where a Romanesque cathedral was built in the 13th century. Italia.it notes that the site has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993. The UNESCO entry adds that the entire population of the Sassi was relocated in the 1950s, and that people began to return in the 1980s. On the date of the evacuation the sources wander: the Ministry of Culture mentions a clearance law of 1952, Lonely Planet Italia says people lived in the Casa Grotta "until 1956", and Italia.it says 1958. UNESCO says only "the 1950s". When you read a precise date, ask where it comes from. How to get to Matera # The nearest airport is Bari Palese, 55 kilometres away according to the Comune's tourist portal, which also lists Brindisi (140 km) and Naples (250 km) and a shuttle between Bari Airport and Matera. The shuttle timetable on the portal is dated, so check it before you travel. Trains hold a surprise. The nearest station on the national network, the same source says, is Ferrandina-Scalo Matera, and from there you continue by road. The direct option from Bari is the FAL (Ferrovie Appulo Lucane) train from Bari Centrale: it stops at Matera Centrale, Matera Sud and Matera Villa Longo. Careful: the FAL station is

t: Palermo street food guide: markets, hours and what to order
d: Capo, Ballarò and Vucciria in Palermo: when to go, what to order (panelle, arancina, sfincione, pani ca meusa) and what it costs, with sources that disagree.
x: Palermo's three great markets look like three versions of the same place, but they keep three different clocks. The Capo and Ballarò are morning markets, the Vucciria is an evening place. Get the hour wrong and you find shutters down or an empty square, and Palermo becomes a hard city to read. This guide lines up the markets, says what to order, and where the sources disagree it says so. In short. Go to the Capo and Ballarò in the morning, when the stalls are working and the fryers are on; leave the Vucciria for the evening. Order panelle and crocchè, an arancina, sfincione and, if you feel brave, pani ca meusa. About €10-15 per person (indicative, in cash) is enough to eat well. Avoid Sunday afternoon for the markets. The Ballarò market in Palermo, between fruit and vegetable stalls and a steady flow of shoppers Photo: Benjamín Núñez González, CC BY-SA 4.0 , Wikimedia Commons Early morning Capo market Enter from Porta Carini and Via Cappuccinelle: panelle, sfincione, arancine, fruit and fish. Late morning Cathedral and Albergheria From the Capo you walk down to the Cathedral and then into the Ballarò district. Midday Ballarò The oldest and largest market: fried things, sfincione and the call of the vendors. Afternoon A pastry shop A cannolo, ideally filled on the spot. Evening Vucciria Piazza Caracciolo comes alive with the grills: stigghiola, pani ca meusa, a glass of something. Which market to choose, and when? # The Comune di Palermo tourism portal lists four names among the most important historic markets: Ballarò, the Vucciria, the Capo and Borgo Vecchio. It likens them to the souks of Muslim cities, with the vendors' call, the «abbanniata», as a soundtrack. For street food, though, the guides give each one a different role. Palermo Food Tours, a tour operator whose text carries a check date of 25 October 2026, sums it up like this: the Capo and Ballarò are daytime markets, busiest from mid-morning and better on a weekday; the Vucciria is quietest by day and comes alive in the dark, when the grills come out. The Capo is in the Seralcadio district, near the Cathedral, and is, it says, one of the easiest to eat through, with panelle, sfincione, arancine and sweets next to fruit and fish. Ballarò, in the Albergheria, is the oldest and largest, and according to the same source the most local. t: Milan in a weekend when it rains: a Plan B itinerary
d: Two rainy days in Milan: the Duomo, Galleria, Museo del Novecento, Castello Sforzesco, Brera and the Last Supper, with hours, indicative prices and closures.
x: Rain does not cancel Milan; it just reshuffles it. The centre is packed with museums, the metro reaches almost everywhere, and the big sights sit in two fairly compact areas. All you need is a sensible order and a few checks on hours and closing days, because that is where a wet weekend really goes wrong. In short. On Saturday stay around Piazza Duomo: Museo del Novecento, the Cathedral and Duomo Museum, Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II. On Sunday move to the Castello Sforzesco and the Pinacoteca di Brera. On Mondays the main museums are closed, and The Last Supper must be booked weeks ahead: it is not a last-minute Plan B. Piazza Duomo seen from above, the starting point of Saturday (a sunny day: in the rain it will look different) Photo: Elena Chochkova, CC BY-SA 3.0 , Wikimedia Commons How much does it actually rain in Milan? # There is no "safe" month. According to the Italian Wikipedia entry on Milan's climate, average annual rainfall is about 920 mm over 82 days, with the peak in autumn, a secondary maximum in spring and a relative low in winter (around 40 mm in February). The same page notes that foggy days are becoming less frequent. These are climate averages, not a forecast: the practical point is that an October or November weekend in Milan can be dry or soaked, so have an indoor plan ready. Rule one: one area per day # The worst rainy-day route is one that crosses half the city at every stop. Here the advantage is clear: Saturday revolves around Piazza Duomo, where the Lombardia.info page puts Palazzo Reale about 120 metres from the Duomo and the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II about 250. On Sunday you shift towards the Castello Sforzesco and Brera. We did not verify the walking distance between the Castello and Brera, so check the map before you leave. Provalo ☔ Piove ☀ Non piove 1. Duomo di Milano: Cathedral and Museum Al coperto # The single ticket for the Cathedral and the Duomo Museum, including the church of San Gottardo in Corte, costs 10 € full price and 5 € reduced, according to the official access page in force since 1 April 2025. On Wednesdays the Museum is closed and the ticket drops to 8 € and 4 €. On a weekend that does not affect you. The Duomo's hours are not straightforward: the ticket office in the Sala delle Colonne is listed as open 9:00 to 18:00, with the last ticket at 17:50, while another line on the same page mentions access through the north portal from 8:00 to 19:00 with last entry at 18:10. Lombardia.info gives 9:00-19:00.

t: Cinque Terre on foot: trails, trains and what is closed
d: Walking the Cinque Terre in late October 2026: which trails show as closed, what the Trekking Card and trains cost, the Via dell'Amore and rail works.
x: cinque-terre--al-via-i-lavori-nelle-stazioni-ferroviarie-d.html UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Portovenere, Cinque Terre and the Islands::https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/826/ CinqueTerre.eu.com (private site), trail status (Italian)::https://www.cinqueterre.eu.com/it/cinque-terre-situazione-sentieri --- The Cinque Terre are best walked with one question in mind: what is open today? Trail status here is not fixed. It moves with the weather, works and crowds, and the only page that counts is the park's. This article puts in order what we read on 30 October 2026 about trails, cards, trains and the Via dell'Amore, says where sources disagree, and leaves you a plan that survives a closure. UNESCO describes the landscape as a steep coast of about 15 km between Levanto and La Spezia, shaped over centuries by dry-stone terraces for vines and olives, which is why trails are maintained, and closed, by precise rules. In short. On 30 October 2026 the park's map shows the Manarola-Corniglia stretch of the Blue Path as closed (skip it by train), while the Via dell'Amore is open only by reservation, one way (Riomaggiore towards Manarola) and from 9 am to 6 pm. To walk you need the Trekking Card (10 € adults, 15 € on high-attendance days) or the Train Card. From 14 November there are weekends with trains suspended for works: always check the official page before leaving. Vernazza seen from above, from a viewpoint on the Blue Path Photo: СССР, CC BY-SA 2.5 ca , Wikimedia Commons What is closed today? All'aperto # The trail network has an official, updated page on the Cinque Terre National Park site, with a weather-alert message (when we opened it, it read "Nessuna allerta", no alert, dated 29 October 2026) and four route categories: tourist, hiking, expert and closed. The Blue Path, the coastal route linking the villages, appears like this: Riomaggiore-Manarola (the Via dell'Amore) as tourist, with a stated 25 minutes; Manarola-Corniglia as closed; Corniglia-Vernazza (1 h 30) and Vernazza-Monterosso (2 h) as routes for experts. A useful cross-check: the private site CinqueTerre.eu.com lists the coastal Manarola-Corniglia stretch as closed "because of a landslide", but its page shows a last edit of 18 May 2026. The two sources agree on the closed stretch, but only the park's is current to the week we are writing. t: Bologna in a day: tortellini, porticoes and a walking plan
d: One day in Bologna under the porticoes: San Petronio, the Clock Tower, Quadrilatero, Archiginnasio and San Luca, with tortellini and official hours.
x: Prenotazione-salita-alla-Torre-degli-Asinelli Bologna Welcome, Clock Tower and Municipal Art Collections (Italian)::https://www.bolognawelcome.com/it/esperienze/300685/Visita-alla-Torre-dell-Orologio-e-alle-Collezioni-Comunali-d-Arte Bologna Welcome, San Luca::https://www.bolognawelcome.com/en/blog/san-luca-eng Basilica di San Petronio, info and hours (Italian)::https://www.basilicadisanpetronio.org/info-e-orari/ Basilica di San Petronio, visits (Italian)::https://www.basilicadisanpetronio.org/visite/ Musei di Bologna, Archiginnasio and Anatomical Theatre (Italian)::https://www.museidibologna.it/archiginnasio/ Dotta Confraternita del Tortellino, the deposited recipe (Italian)::https://www.confraternitadeltortellino.it/la-ricetta-depositata/ Bologna Welcome, ragù alla bolognese (Accademia Italiana della Cucina)::https://www.bolognawelcome.com/en/other/recipes-and-typical-products/ragu-alla-bolognese-2 Emilia Romagna Tourism, Quadrilatero del gusto (Italian)::https://emiliaromagnaturismo.it/it/itinerari/quadrilatero-del-gusto --- Bologna is walked with a roof over your head. The porticoes work as a corridor between stops and, if the weather turns, the plan barely changes. This itinerary puts one walking day in order across square, towers, market and porticoes, with tortellini at the centre, and says where hours are seasonal, where sources disagree and what is closed right now. In short. Morning around Piazza Maggiore, San Petronio (free entry) and the Clock Tower; lunch in the Quadrilatero; early afternoon at the Archiginnasio; if you have energy left, the San Luca portico. When we opened the official booking page, the Asinelli Tower was listed as closed for maintenance: the Clock Tower is the alternative it points to. The art collections are closed on Mondays. The paid route through three chapels costs 5 €. 10:00 am Clock Tower Reservation required; from September to February the first entry is at 10:00 am. Lunch Quadrilatero Via Clavature, Drapperie, Pescherie Vecchie: cured meats, fresh pasta and stalls to eat at. Afternoon Archiginnasio and Anatomical Theatre The old university seat: audioguide visit, entries every 10 minutes. Late San Luca portico Optional, uphill: more than 2 km of slope or steps. t: What to eat in Catania: 10 tastes in order of the day
d: Arancino, granita with brioche, pasta alla Norma, horse meat and Sant'Agata sweets: what to order in Catania, when, and roughly what it costs.
x: Eating in Catania is not solved with a restaurant: it is solved with a well-built day. You start with a granita, pass through the market, have something fried for lunch and finish with a pasta that here has an opera-house name. This guide puts the tastings in the order that makes sense, tells you when to order them, what they cost on average and what is better left alone. In short. Morning: granita and brioche. Mid-morning: fish market and street food. Lunch: arancino and pasta alla Norma. Afternoon: sweets. Evening: horse meat or fish, if you like. Indicative average prices: €18-33 for a day of tastings, dinner at a restaurant excluded. Morning Granita with brioche Almond, pistachio, coffee or lemon, with Sicilian brioche. About €4. Mid-morning Fish market and surroundings Watch the market and taste standing up. Lunch Arancino and pasta alla Norma In Catania the fried one is masculine; Norma is the first course not to skip. Afternoon Cannolo and sweets Sheep's ricotta and marzipan. Evening Horse meat or fish One choice, not both. 1. Granita and brioche # The Catanese breakfast is granita (water, sugar and fruit) with a Sicilian brioche, leavened with eggs and scented with vanilla or citrus. The flavours to start from are almond, pistachio, coffee and lemon. Travel365 recommends trying almond first; for coffee, the same source suggests having it with brioche and whipped cream. If you are short on time, pick just one flavour and do not argue with the menu. Indicative average cost: about €4. 2. Seltz with lemon and salt # At the city's kiosks they drink a seltz made with lemon juice, sparkling water, salt and a pinch of bicarbonate. It sounds odd until it is hot. About €2: Do Eat Better Experience quotes €1.50-2 and says to drink it right away while it is still foaming, because waiting flattens the fizz. 3. The fish market and its street food # The fish market, which locals call "a piscaria", is a few steps from Piazza Duomo, near the Fountain of the Seven Channels. You do not have to buy anything: just walking through it is a taste of the city. Around it you find kiosks and small places selling food to eat standing up. According to Do Eat Better Experience, the closest street food is the paper cone of fried fish at Scirocco Sicilian Fish Lab (€9, with a long queue around lunchtime); Travel365 gives an average of €7 per person for the same place. t: Venice without the crowds: when to go and where to eat
d: How to visit Venice without the crowds: the access fee, vaporetto fares, Rialto market hours and bacari, with the sources' disagreements flagged.
x: Venice is not a city to "do": it is a city to cross in a certain order, at certain hours. The problem is not the city, it is the moment you arrive. This guide puts together what the official pages of the City and of AVM say (access fee, vaporetto, rules of conduct) with what tourism sites say about hours, quieter districts and bacari, flagging every time where sources disagree. Most of the sources are in Italian, so the names of pages and terms are given as they appear. In short. Today there is no access fee to enter Venice (the 2026 trial ended on 26 July; in 2027 it returns on fixed days between March and August, from 8:30 to 16:30). To avoid the crowds go early in the morning or after sunset, put the middle of the day in Cannaregio and Castello, and eat at the counter in a bacaro rather than at the tables around San Marco. For vaporetto and markets always check the official pages: prices and days change. Early morning Rialto: market and Erbaria The market gives its best in the first part of the morning; fruit and vegetables, according to two sites, close at 13:30. Mid-morning Cannaregio Fondamenta, canals and the ghetto: here the city runs at the pace of its residents. Lunch A bacaro Cicchetti standing at the counter, an ombra of wine and off you go: the Venetian lunch is short. Early afternoon Castello The least touristy district according to local sites: Via Garibaldi, the gardens and the Arsenale. Afternoon Vaporetto to the Giudecca A single long ride, to look at the city from the water. Evening Cannaregio or Dorsoduro After sunset many day visitors have already left. Do I have to pay to enter Venice? # The access fee is the most frequent question, and it is also where the sources contradict each other. The City of Venice's information page, updated on 13 March 2026, still describes the 2026 calendar: from 3 April to 26 July, for 60 non-consecutive days. The official fee site (cda.ve.it), on the other hand, states at the top that the 2026 trial has ended and that from 27 July 2026 the fee does not apply: you can visit Venice without any payment or request for exemption. This second statement is the most recent, and it matches today's date: no fee to pay. For the future, the same site lists the 2027 days: March 26, 27, 28, 29; April 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 11, 16, 17, 18 and 23 to 30; May 1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 14, 15, 16, 21, 22, 23 and 28 to 31; June 1 to 6, 11, 12, 13, 18, 19, 20, 25, 26, 27; July 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 11, 16, 17, 18, 23, 24, 25, 30, 31; August 1, 6, 7,

t: One day in Lecce: baroque, pasticciotto and walking lanes
d: A walking itinerary for one day in Lecce: Roman amphitheatre, Duomo, Santa Croce, the castle and a pasticciotto, with hours and prices from official sources.
x: Lecce is a city to walk with your chin up. Lecce baroque does not come across in a photo: it needs a slow pace, pale stone that changes colour with the light, and a sweet stop or two. This itinerary puts one walking day in order, with few stops and the reason for each, and says plainly where hours change with the season. In short. Breakfast with a pasticciotto, the amphitheatre in Piazza Sant'Oronzo and the Faggiano museum in the morning, the castle around midday, the baroque route (Duomo, Santa Croce) in the afternoon. From October to March the churches close at 6 pm and the amphitheatre at about 3:30 pm, so the order of the stops matters. Avoid Mondays. Breakfast Pasticciotto in a café in the centre Pastry and custard, even better lukewarm. It is the Salento morning ritual. 9:30 am Roman amphitheatre Piazza Sant'Oronzo: in autumn and winter it opens early and closes early, so it goes first. 10:45 am Faggiano museum Open every day until 8 pm: the wildcard stop. Entry around 5 €. 12:30 pm Charles V Castle Entry only on a guided tour of about 50 minutes, at fixed times. Lunch Inner streets A simple Salento dish, away from the main squares. 2:30 pm Duomo, Santa Croce and churches Single ticket: get in by 5:45 pm, because everything closes at 6. Provalo ☔ Piove ☀ Non piove Before you go: days and hours to check All'aperto # You can see Lecce in a day only if the opening hours line up, and in autumn they do not line up on their own. The churches on the baroque route are open every day from 9 am to 9 pm according to the official site, but between October and March they close at 6 pm, with entry allowed until 15 minutes before. The amphitheatre, on the Ministry of Culture site, is listed as closed on Monday and open 9 am to 3:30 pm on winter hours; the online ticket office, when consulted, showed 9 am to 3 pm for ticket sales and 9 am to 3:30 pm for the public. The castle is open Tuesday to Sunday. The practical consequence is simple: whatever closes early (the amphitheatre, the castle tour) goes in the morning, whatever stays open until evening (the churches, the Faggiano museum) goes in the afternoon. If Monday is the only day you have, drop the amphitheatre and the castle and keep the baroque route and the Faggiano. Morning: breakfast with a pasticciotto All'aperto # Start where locals start. t: Florence in 48 hours without pointless queues
d: Two days in Florence in a sensible order: Duomo and Dome, Accademia, Uffizi. Hours, closing days, prices and bookings read on the official sites.
x: Florence goes wrong in two ways: standing in line in the sun outside a museum, or running back and forth because you never looked at the calendar. In 48 hours you can avoid both if you think about three things: which days are closed, what has to be booked at a fixed time, and what you can leave open. This itinerary puts the Duomo and the Accademia on the first day and the Uffizi on the second. In short. Day 1: the Brunelleschi Dome (at a booked time), the Duomo and the Galleria dell'Accademia. Day 2: the Uffizi, ideally with a ticket already bought, then Florence on foot. Never on a Monday: the Uffizi and the Accademia are closed. Check strike notices and free days. Day 1 · morning Brunelleschi Dome Time fixed at purchase, 5 minutes' tolerance, ID required. There are 463 steps. Day 1 · late morning Cathedral and Piazza del Duomo The Cathedral is free; the other monuments need the Pass. Day 1 · afternoon Galleria dell'Accademia The David and more. Open until 6:50 pm, but ticket sales stop 30 minutes earlier. Day 2 · morning Uffizi Named ticket, best bought in advance. Open from 8:15 am. Day 2 · afternoon Florence on foot No tickets: the rest is a stroll. Quale giorno ti serve? Entrambi Giorno 1 Giorno 2 Day 1: Duomo, Dome and Accademia # You start where the Pass forces you to be on time: the Dome. The Brunelleschi Pass includes entry to the Baptistery of San Giovanni, Giotto's Bell Tower, the Dome, the Museo dell'Opera del Duomo and the basilica of Santa Reparata, with one entry per monument, valid for 3 calendar days. Validity starts from the date chosen for the Dome, and the booked day and time cannot be changed: choose carefully. The other monuments can be visited with no time restriction. On the Dome, the official site is clear: the climb takes about 45 minutes, there are 463 steps and no lift, it is not recommended for people with heart problems, vertigo or claustrophobia, and since 1 March 2025 you must show an ID document with your ticket. Backpacks and medium or large bags go in the cloakroom before entering, and the entrance is the Porta della Mandorla, on the north side of the Cathedral. The site allows at most 5 minutes early or late compared with the time you chose. After the Dome, the Cathedral is free to enter and needs no Pass. t: Catania fish market: hours, what to see and how to visit
d: Indicative hours, when to go, what to look at and what to avoid at the Catania fish market, a few steps from Piazza Duomo.
x: The Catania fish market is not an attraction set up for tourists: it is a market that works every morning, loud, wet and beautiful. To visit it well you need a few rules: the right time, the right shoes and an idea of what to look at. Here you get the hours with the disagreements between sources, how to get there, what to do in the rain and the mistakes to skip. In short. Go early in the morning, Monday to Saturday, in closed non-slip shoes. Give the market 30-60 minutes and, if you want to eat, another hour nearby. Sunday is closed. Hours: about 7 am-2 pm for three sources out of four, 8 am-2:30 pm for the fourth. Before 10 Entrance from the Piazza Duomo side The stalls are fully stocked and the light is better. Mid-morning Walk between the stalls Swordfish, tuna, sea bream, sea urchins, octopus. Edges Fruit and vegetables Oranges, broccoli, artichokes: calmer. Afterwards Tastings standing up Street food nearby. Stalls and shoppers at Catania's fish market in the morning Photo: Effems, CC0 , Wikimedia Commons Hours: what we know and what we do not # The sources we consulted agree on two points: the market is open Monday to Saturday and closed on Sunday. On exact hours they differ: Nomado Travel, Loving Sicilia and Do Eat Better Experience say about 7 am to 2 pm, Siviaggia says 8 am to 2:30 pm. No official source settles it, because we did not find an open, consultable one from the city council. That is why the practical rule is the safest one: arrive by mid-morning. After noon some stalls are already packing up, and the best produce is gone. When to go, really # The best window is before 10: full choice and less heat, especially in summer. Here too the sources do not agree on the peak: for Nomado Travel the crowd is at its densest between 8:30 and 10:30, for Loving Sicilia between 10 and 12. After 11 the character changes: Nomado Travel writes that vendors are trying to clear stock, so prices may drop but choice shrinks; Do Eat Better Experience says that by around 11:30 the best swordfish cuts are already sold. Around 12:30-1 pm several stalls are dismantled (Nomado Travel and Loving Sicilia); it is a quiet moment for a second pass without the crowd. If you want to take photos, choose a weekday and make eye contact with the vendors before shooting. How to get there # The market is in the historic centre, a few metres from Piazza Duomo and near the fountain that Siviaggia calls the Fountain of the Seven Channels and Nomado Travel calls the Amenano fountai

t: What to do in Catania when it rains: 7 indoor ideas
d: Rain in Catania? Seven places under a roof, a sensible order to see them and how to rewrite your day without wasting the afternoon.
x: In Catania rain does not ruin the day: it moves it. The historic centre is compact, distances between stops are short and many of the most interesting places are indoors. You only need a sensible order, so you do not cross half the city in the downpour. In short. Keep the stops close, alternate an indoor place with a short outdoor stretch, and check opening hours: museums and monuments change days and time slots. The Achillean Baths, for instance, are listed as open only until 2:00 pm, so they belong in the morning. Castello Ursino, one of Catania's indoor stops Photo: Cayambe, CC BY-SA 4.0 , Wikimedia Commons When does it actually rain in Catania? # Rain is not spread evenly through the year. One climate page we read lists 7 rainy days in October, 5 in November and 8 in each of December and January, against 1 in June and 1 in July. A second page with a rainfall table puts October at the top with 84 mm, followed by September with 77 mm, and gives a yearly total around 600 mm; the same page, however, says in its text that November is the wettest month, so read the numbers as orders of magnitude. The practical message is simple: from October to January an indoor plan is not an exception, it is part of the trip. If you travel in those months, do not build a day around a single outdoor activity. Plan two interchangeable half days: one for sun and one for rain. The rainy one is this page. First rule: stay in one area # The worst route in the rain is the one that jumps from one end of the city to the other. Pick one area and fill it: the stretch between Via Etnea, Piazza Duomo and the fish market is the most comfortable, because everything is a few minutes on foot. Provalo ☔ Piove ☀ Non piove 1. Teatro Massimo Bellini Al coperto # The theatre named after Vincenzo Bellini is one of the city's landmark places, right in the centre. According to Italia.it it opened on 31 May 1890 with Bellini's Norma , and guided tours can be booked. Tour times and prices do not appear on the pages we opened, so ask the theatre. Mind the address: Italia.it gives Via Giuseppe Perrotta 12, while another source places the theatre on Piazza Vincenzo Bellini. The two do not match, so trust your map and the theatre's own website. 2. Castello Ursino and the civic museum Al coperto # The Swabian-era castle was built between 1239 and 1250 under Frederick II, and the civic museum has been inside it since 1934. Volcanic activity and earthquakes mean it now stands about a kilometre from the sea

t: Rome in two days: an itinerary that does not wear you out
d: Two days in Rome in a sensible order: stops grouped by area, hours to check and how not to spend the day in a queue.
x: You can see Rome in two days if you accept one rule: do not try to see everything. The city is made of layers, and the more you try to cover it, the more time you spend between stops. The secret is to group it by area and to decide in advance which two or three things need a ticket, a time slot or a queue. In short. Day one: ancient Rome (Colosseum, Forum, Palatine, then Monti and the Capitoline Hill). Day two: the Vatican in the morning, then Pantheon, Navona, Trevi and Trastevere. From late October the Colosseum park closes at 16:30 (4:30 pm), so plan the archaeology for the morning. Day 1 · morning Colosseum, Forum and Palatine A single route: book ahead to avoid the queue. Day 1 · lunch Monti A more genuine neighbourhood a few minutes from the Colosseum. Day 1 · afternoon Capitoline Hill and the centre The view over the Forum, then on foot into the historic centre. Day 2 · morning Vatican Museums and St Peter's To be booked, and the longest part of the day. Day 2 · afternoon Pantheon, Navona, Trevi All close, a few minutes' walk apart. Day 2 · evening Trastevere A stroll with no plan. Consiglio Put the booked stops on the same day and keep the other one free: if it rains or you are tired, you move the free part, not the one with a ticket. Quale giorno ti serve? Entrambi Giorno 1 Giorno 2 The Colosseum seen from the Roman Forum Photo: Roma1314, CC BY-SA 3.0 , Wikimedia Commons The façade of the Pantheon in Rome Photo: NikonZ7II, CC BY-SA 4.0 , Wikimedia Commons Day 1: ancient Rome # Morning: Colosseum, Forum and Palatine. They are close and covered by one ticket. On the park's official site the standard ticket is valid for 24 hours and gives one entry to the Colosseum (first and second tier, no arena) and one entry to the Roman Forum and Palatine. That means you can split the visit: the Colosseum when it opens, the Forum and Palatine after lunch, as long as you stay inside the 24 hours. Hours matter. According to the park's page, from 25 October 2026 to 28 February 2027 the site is open 8:30 to 16:30, with last entry at 15:30; the Colosseum opens at 8:30, while the Forum and Palatine open at 9:00. In practice, in winter the archaeological afternoon is short: do the main block in the morning. Lunch around Monti. A few minutes' walk from the Colosseum, it is a neighbourhood with less touristy places than the area immediately around the monuments. t: One day in Ortigia: a walking itinerary, without rushing
d: How to see Ortigia in a day: order of the stops, where to slow down and what to leave out so it does not turn into a marathon.
x: Ortigia is small, and that is exactly why it is easy to get wrong: you cross it in a rush trying to see everything and leave feeling you have not really looked at it. This itinerary does the opposite. Few stops, an order that makes sense and room to pause. In short. Market in the morning, Duomo and square around midday, seafront and the Fountain of Arethusa in the late afternoon. The rest you choose by mood. Be careful with Castello Maniace: the opening hours we found contradict each other, so do not make it the fixed point of your day. Morning Ortigia market The starting point: arrive early, taste standing up and leave before the crowd. Late morning Duomo and square The Greek temple inside the Baroque cathedral, and five minutes on the square. Lunch Side streets Two blocks from the square are enough to change quality and prices. Early afternoon Inner streets and the Giudecca Without a plan, keeping an eye out for guided visits. Late afternoon Fountain of Arethusa and seafront As far as Castello Maniace, in the low light. A che ora sei a Ortigia? 09:00 Ortigia seen from the sea, with its seafront and waterside houses Photo: Darold Massaro, CC0 , Wikimedia Commons Getting there # Ortigia is the island that forms the historic centre of Syracuse: according to Italia.it it measures a little over one square kilometre and is linked to the city by two bridges, Ponte Umbertino and Ponte Santa Lucia. From Catania the simplest way is the train to Siracusa. Two timetable pages we read do not agree on the details: one lists 33 trains, the first at 6:06 and the last at 21:29, with journeys between 1h07 and 1h23; the other lists 12 direct trains, from 10:39 to 20:20, with an average of 1h18 and a minimum of 1h05, a train ticket from about 9 EUR and a bus from about 5 EUR (indicative averages). The gap probably depends on the day each page was captured: check the real timetable the evening before. If you plan to arrive by car, remember there is a restricted traffic zone (ZTL) across the whole island. The page we read, last updated in 2020 and therefore to be taken with caution, lists three camera gates (Santa Lucia, Via Vittorio Veneto, Via dei Mille) and different hours for summer and winter, with tighter restrictions at weekends and in the evening. Hotel and B&B guests enter with a pass issued through their accommodation. For a single day it is not worth it: arrive by train, or leave the car outside and cross on foot. t: AI travel itineraries: what works and what does not
d: How to use AI to plan a trip without letting it invent places that do not exist: what to ask, what to check and why real places matter.
x: Asking an AI "plan me three days in Palermo" always works, in the sense that an answer arrives. The point is another: is it right? A good itinerary is not a well-written list, it is a sequence of real places, open, reachable in the order it proposes. And that is where things get complicated. In short. AI is excellent at putting things in order and giving ideas, mediocre when it has to guarantee that a place exists and is open. The difference is made by the real data under the answer and by the check you do before you leave. What AI does well # It orders. It turns ten scattered ideas into a day with a logical thread. It adapts. If you say "I am with kids" or "I only have half a day", the angle changes. It explains. It tells you why a place is worth it, not just where it is. It rewrites. If a ticket falls through or it rains, it redoes the programme in seconds. What it does badly # It invents with confidence. A generic model can suggest a restaurant that has closed, a museum that does not exist, a wrong opening time. It ignores geography. It can line up stops that are half an hour apart on foot on the map. It does not know it is raining today. Unless it receives the data, it does not adapt the programme to the day. It flattens the rules. Information that changes by season, weekday or event is often squeezed into one sentence that is true "in general". Why does it happen? The short version # A paper by researchers at OpenAI and Georgia Tech describes hallucinations as plausible but false statements. According to the authors they persist because training and evaluation reward guessing more than admitting uncertainty: on a right-or-wrong test, an "I don't know" scores zero while a guess can score a point. It is not a flaw of one product: it is a behaviour to know about and work around with method. Anthropic's guide to reducing hallucinations reaches the same conclusion from the practical side: its techniques significantly reduce errors but do not eliminate them, and critical information should always be validated. How to use it without getting hurt # Give precise context: area, days, pace, who you travel with. Ask for close stops, grouped by neighbourhood. Give the AI permission not to know. Anthropic's guide lists this as the first step: allowing the model to say it does not know the answer can sharply reduce false information.
